title: How AI Search Finds Things
description: The index inside most vector databases: points on a stack of graphs, sparse at the top and dense at the bottom. A search takes long jumps up high, drops down, and finds the closest matches after checking only a small fraction of the points.
long_description:
Every point lives on the bottom layer. Each layer above keeps only about a fifth of the points below it, picked at random, so the upper layers are sparse and their links are long jumps across the map.

A search enters at the top, hops greedily toward the target, drops a layer, and repeats with finer steps. At the bottom it widens into a small beam search to collect the closest few. The corner shows how many points it actually measured — usually a quarter or less — and how often that matched the exact answer.

This is HNSW (Malkov & Yashunin, 2016), the method most vector databases use to find “things like this” for chatbots and image search. The graphs here are built the way the paper describes.
action_hints: run a search and follow it down the layers
add twenty points and watch them link in
rebuild the whole graph with new random layers
